header:
Date: 2026-05-03
Time: 15:00 - 15:51 UTC
Duration: 51 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Ortiz (Redwood SE), Priya Narang (Redwood SE), Anita Rao (Crestline Head of Procurement), Marcus Bell (Crestline Infosec), Sofia Kim (Crestline Legal), Diego Alvarez (Crestline Platform)
summary: Redwood presented commercial pilot terms and walked through technical egress and KMS options. Customer raised data residency and egress fee concerns and asked for an end-to-end pilot benchmark. Legal outlined a few DPA exceptions; procurement pushed for price tiering for pilot vs production. Next: Redwood to send redlines, SE to run benchmark, customer to provide traffic samples and DPA redlines.
topics: SLA targets for pilot vs production
Egress fees and data residency implications
Pilot success criteria and token projections
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'll do a quick intro. I'm Maya from Redwood, and with me are Liam and Priya on the technical side.
[00:10] Anita Rao: Hi all, Anita here. We're hoping to, um, get clarity on two things today — the contract redlines and the egress/billing questions before we move pilot forward.
[00:22] Liam Ortiz: Great, thanks Anita. We'll aim to cover both. Quick agenda: commercial terms (MSA/DPA), security/KMS options, then a technical readout on how billing/egress would look.
[00:32] Sofia Kim: Quick note from legal — we'll be flagging some standard DPA exceptions around subprocessors and subprocessor notifications.
[00:38] Maya Chen: Noted. We'll start with the MSA overview. The pilot is typically a short 30‑60 day engagement with a capped usage estimate and a discounted pilot rate. For production we have tiered pricing and reserved capacity options.
[00:51] Marcus Bell: When you say reserved capacity — can you remind us how that affects egress charges? Our treasury team is very sensitive to variable fees.
[01:02] Priya Narang: Sure — reserved (Dedicated) gives you predictable throughput and you can apply private networking. Egress, meaning data out of the region or out to third parties, is billed separately; we can show a projection based on your estimated token volumes.
[01:18] Diego Alvarez: Are egress fees applied per GB or per token? We have a weird mix of embeddings traffic and generation.
[01:26] Liam Ortiz: Good question. For most customers we break costs down: per‑token generation + optional per‑GB egress for model artifacts or large bulk dumps. Embeddings are billed per‑embedding unit. For the pilot we can set a capped egress allowance to avoid surprise charges.
[01:40] Anita Rao: Capped allowance sounds promising; procurement will need a clear escalation path if we exceed pilot caps.
[01:46] Maya Chen: Absolutely — we include an overage notification plan and can pause or throttle to avoid surprises.
[01:52] Sofia Kim: On the DPA side — we want to know which subprocessors you use, are you using any third‑party monitoring, and what access logs look like.
[02:01] Priya Narang: We can share a subprocessor list. Runtime logs are available, and for Private deployments we also support customer‑managed logging and audit log retention policies. Note: some of the infra tooling names might be slightly off in the transcript, e.g., K-V cash is kv cache, but we'll attach the formal docs.
[02:20] Marcus Bell: Also, KMS options — do you support customer‑managed keys (bring your own key) and HSM?
[02:27] Liam Ortiz: Yes, we support KMS integrations including AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and external HSM via PKCS#11 in our Private offering. For Hosted we offer envelope encryption + optional KEK integration.
[02:38] Diego Alvarez: If we bring our own key, does that eliminate Redwood access to plaintext during inference?
[02:44] Priya Narang: Not entirely — BYOK restricts certain cloud provider access, but the inference runtime still needs to decrypt to serve model tokens unless you use a fully isolated on‑prem package. We can walk through a threat model.
[02:58] Anita Rao: Ok that clarifies. From a procurement standpoint we also need to lock SLA targets — for pilot is 99% availability ok? Our user flows are not critical in pilot but latency matters for UX.
[03:10] Liam Ortiz: For pilot we typically aim for SLOs rather than strict SLA—like 95–99% availability depending on configuration. For Dedicated with an SLA we can commit to the 99.9% uptime tier but that comes with reserved capacity and a different pricing band.
[03:29] Sofia Kim: Any indemnity or data residency clauses we should note? We need data residency in EU for specific workloads.
[03:36] Maya Chen: We support region pinning in hosted and private. For EU residency we can pin model serving to eu-west-1 or run Private inside your VPC. Indemnity language follows standard vendor terms; we can surface the specifics in the redline.
[03:50] Marcus Bell: There was a mention in your docs about automatic fallback to cheaper model variants if capacity is constrained — does that pose a risk for data going to a different region?
[03:59] Liam Ortiz: Fallbacks are configurable by policy — you can restrict fallbacks to same‑region, same‑residency models. We'll include those routing policy settings in the runbook.
[04:12] Anita Rao: Pricing: procurement wants a two‑tiered approach — pilot at discounted rate, and then production committed monthly volumes. Can you commit to price protection for 90 days post‑pilot?
[04:23] Maya Chen: We can do a 90‑day price protection window on committed rates for the production offer if you sign within that period.
[04:29] Diego Alvarez: For the benchmark — we want a 24h run using our sample corpus to measure latency tail and cost per 1M tokens. Is that what you suggested?
[04:38] Liam Ortiz: Yep, we'll run a 24h continuous synthetic or replayed traffic job; we'll give p50/p90/p99 latency and per‑token cost breakdown. We will also include KV cache hit rates because that affects cost.
[04:50] Sofia Kim: On the DPA exception list, the big ask is narrow subprocessors notification window, and stronger deletion guarantees for logs. Can Redwood commit to deletion upon request for pilot data?
[05:01] Maya Chen: For Hosted, we have standard retention windows; for pilot we can agree to a specific retention and deletion process documented in the DPA addendum. For Private deployment, deletion is under customer control.
[05:12] Anita Rao: Good. Procurement will also need an escalations contact and a stub for a limited liability cap for the pilot.
[05:19] Maya Chen: We'll propose language for a limited liability cap tied to fees paid during the pilot.
[05:23] Marcus Bell: A couple of technical clarifications: what happens if we want to use our model variants or custom tokenizers, any extra charges?
[05:31] Liam Ortiz: Custom models are supported — hosting custom weights on Dedicated/Private has storage and inference charges. Tokenizer differences can sometimes affect tokenization count, we can map your tokenizer and show adjusted token projections.
[05:46] [06:00] (crosstalk, short pause)
[06:10] Maya Chen: I'm going to unmute Liam for a technical deep dive real quick. Liam?
[06:15] Liam Ortiz: Thanks. Quick architecture: for Hosted we run inference on Redwood multitenant clusters with continuous batching and KV caching. For Dedicated, you get a reserved GPU pool. We do model kernel selection optimizations. The important part for egress is the artifact transfer — model weights or export snapshots are GB scale; inference token traffic is not usually called egress unless you pull full transcripts out.
[06:40] Diego Alvarez: So user transcripts — if we pull logs for e-discovery, that's egress?
[06:46] Liam Ortiz: Yes, large bulk export of transcripts or embeddings is billed per GB egress. Small per-request responses are accounted for in token billing.
[06:55] Marcus Bell: And audit logs — are they stored in your control plane by default? Can we forward to our SIEM?
[07:03] Priya Narang: We store inferred logs in the control plane with configurable retention; yes you can forward to your SIEM via forwarders or route logs to your VPC.
[07:12] Sofia Kim: Back to DPA: our legal team asks for subprocessor notification 30 days prior to onboarding new subprocessors — your standard window is 60?
[07:21] Maya Chen: Our standard public subprocessor notice is 60 days but we can discuss contractually limiting that for this engagement.
[07:28] Anita Rao: For procurement signoff we'll need an internal cost model sheet showing pilot costs, egress scenarios, and a worst‑case estimate.
[07:36] Maya Chen: We'll attach a conservative worst‑case with the redline MSA and the pricing sheet.
[07:40] Liam Ortiz: One more technical note: if you use prefix caching heavily, you could significantly reduce per‑token costs; we'll show cache hit simulation in the benchmark.
[07:49] Diego Alvarez: How do you measure cache hits — is it per conversation or per prompt?
[07:53] Liam Ortiz: It's measured by KV cache key reuse over sequences; in practice it's across sessions that repeat prompts. We'll provide the hit rate logs.
[08:02] (short pause, typing)
[08:10] Sofia Kim: On the MSA redlines — are you open to a mutual SaaS indemnity, or do you expect standard vendor indemnity?
[08:18] Maya Chen: Standard vendor indemnity but we're open on some points for enterprise deals; I'll flag specifics in the redline.
[08:24] Anita Rao: Timeline question: procurement wants pilot contract signed by 2026‑05‑10 to start the week of 2026‑05‑17. Is that feasible?
[08:32] Maya Chen: Feasible if we get the DPA exceptions back quickly. Our legal can turn around a redline within 3 business days after you send exceptions.
[08:40] Sofia Kim: We'll send our initial DPA redlines by tomorrow COB.
[08:44] Marcus Bell: A security ask — do you have SOC 2 Type II, and do you offer penetration test reports under NDA?
[08:50] Priya Narang: Yes, SOC 2 Type II. We can provide pen test summaries under an NDA and provide SOC report access via our secure portal.
[08:58] Diego Alvarez: For the benchmark infrastructure: will you be able to run it against our VPC or only against hosted endpoints?
[09:05] Liam Ortiz: We can run both. For full fidelity we prefer running a Private or Dedicated test inside your VPC; for a quick check we'll use hosted with masked traffic.
[09:16] Anita Rao: Procurement will need the pilot pricing cap and a clause that the pilot caps cannot be exceeded without written approvals.
[09:24] Maya Chen: We'll include an approval gating mechanism in the SOW and pilot addendum.
[09:30] (brief silence)
[09:36] Maya Chen: Ok, wrapping up — recap: Redwood will send the redlined MSA & DPA, pricing sheet, and an SOW for pilot with capped egress. SEs will run a 24h benchmark with customer sample once Diego provides sample traffic. Customer legal will send DPA exceptions.
[09:54] Anita Rao: Sounds good. Also please include a single point of contact for escalations.
[10:00] Maya Chen: Will do — I'll include names and escalation ladder.
[10:04] Sofia Kim: We'll review redlines and follow up with specifics.
[10:07] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up by email with the docs and schedule the benchmark.
[10:12] (meeting ends)

Notes: transcript contains occasional mis‑transcriptions e.g., "k-v cash" for KV cache, "VBP" for VPC, "SAMEL" for SAML. Formal attachments to be sent post-call: MSA+DPA redline, pricing sheet, runbook, SOC2 summary, benchmark template.
